notes.body:
Machine learning is linear algebra at scale, so we build the objects by hand before they get big. A vector is an ordered list of numbers — [1,2,3] — which you can read two ways: as a point in space (coordinates) or as an arrow from the origin (direction and magnitude). Both readings matter: features of a network event (packet count, byte count, duration) form a vector, and the classifier treats it as a point to be separated or a direction to be measured. Two operations. Addition is component-wise: [1,2,3] + [4,5,6] = [1+4, 2+5, 3+6] = [5,7,9] — geometrically, place the arrows head-to-tail. Scalar multiplication scales every component: 2 × [1,2,3] = [2,4,6] — same direction, twice as long (negative scalars reverse direction). Worked security example: an event's feature vector is [packets=120, bytes=84000, duration_s=60]. Normalize crudely by dividing by [1000, 100000, 3600]... component-wise division isn't a vector operation, but scaling is: (1/1000)×[120, 84000, 60] is not right either — the honest move is scaling each feature to comparable ranges before ML, because raw features with wildly different scales (bytes vs seconds) let the biggest number dominate every distance computation. That preprocessing step — putting features on comparable scales — is applied linear algebra, and skipping it is the most common 'the model doesn't work' root cause in ML-for-security projects. The zero vector [0,0,0] is the origin; subtracting vectors gives the displacement between points: [4,5,6]−[1,2,3] = [3,3,3]. Keep both readings (point and arrow) alive: 'distance between events' uses the point reading, 'direction of change' uses the arrow reading. Common mistake: treating vectors as mere lists. The operations — add, scale, dot (next note) — are what make them vectors; a list you never add or dot is just storage.

Feature engineering is vector design, and it is where security ML is won or lost. Worked: you are building a detector for suspicious PowerShell. Raw input: the command string. Features you might extract: length (characters), entropy of the string, count of suspicious tokens (IEX, DownloadString, -EncodedCommand), number of special characters, max token length. One command becomes [length=212, entropy=4.8, sus_tokens=3, special=31, max_tok=44] — a 5D vector. Two commands' vectors can now be dotted, distanced, and classified. The design decisions are the modeling: including entropy captures obfuscation; counting specific tokens captures known-bad patterns; normalizing (length/1000, entropy/8) keeps scales comparable. Bad features (process ID, timestamp) add noise dimensions the classifier must learn to ignore — and in high dimensions, noise is where evasion lives. The discipline: every feature needs a reason ('obfuscated commands have high entropy'), documented with the vector schema. When the detector fails, the first suspect is the features, not the algorithm. Vectors are the interface between your domain knowledge and the math — design them deliberately.
notes.title: Vectors: points, arrows, and feature vectors

notes.body:
The dot product is the single most-used operation in machine learning — attention mechanisms, similarity search, and classifier scores are all dot products wearing costumes. Definition: a·b = Σ aᵢbᵢ — multiply component-wise, add up. Worked: [1,2,3]·[4,5,6] = 1×4 + 2×5 + 3×6 = 4 + 10 + 18 = 32. Geometric meaning: a·b = |a||b|cos θ — the product of lengths times the cosine of the angle between them. So the dot product measures alignment: large positive means the vectors point the same way, zero means perpendicular, negative means opposed. This gives cosine similarity, the workhorse of embeddings and document comparison: cos θ = (a·b)/(|a|·|b|), where |a| = √(a·a) is the length. Worked: a=[1,2,3], b=[4,5,6]. |a| = √(1+4+9) = √14 ≈ 3.742. |b| = √(16+25+36) = √77 ≈ 8.775. cos θ = 32/(3.742×8.775) = 32/32.83 ≈ 0.975 — nearly parallel, strongly aligned. Cosine similarity ignores magnitude: [1,1] and [100,100] have cosine 1.0 — same direction, different sizes. That is a feature for text ('long document about malware' vs 'short note about malware' share direction) and a trap for security features (a 10-packet scan and a 10,000-packet flood point the same way but are very different events — normalize or use Euclidean distance when magnitude matters). Worked security example: compare two process behavior vectors — process A: [file_writes=5, net_conns=2, registry_edits=8], process B: [50, 20, 80]. Cosine similarity: dot = 250+40+640 = 930; |A| = √(25+4+64)=√93≈9.64; |B| = √(2500+400+6400)=√9300≈96.44; cos = 930/(9.64×96.44) = 930/929.7 ≈ 1.0 — identical behavior shape at different scale (B does everything 10× more). An analyst sees 'same pattern, scaled up' — possibly the same malware family with a loop count change. Common mistake: using cosine similarity when magnitude is the signal. Choose the similarity to match the question: direction → cosine; position → Euclidean distance.

Here is why dot products run modern AI: attention is dot-product similarity. In a transformer, each token asks 'which other tokens should I pay attention to?' by dotting its query vector against every token's key vector — high dot product means high relevance, and the softmax turns those scores into weights. Conceptually it is the same operation as your [1,2,3] dot [4,5,6] = 32, scaled to thousands of dimensions and millions of pairs. The security relevance is twofold. First, interpretability: attention weights show what the model 'looked at' — when your AI triage copilot summarizes an alert, attention patterns (where available) hint at which inputs drove the output, a debugging aid for hallucinations. Second, cost: attention is quadratic in sequence length (every token dots every other), which is why long-context inference is expensive and why prompt-injection via long pasted content has a compute cost to the attacker too. You do not need the transformer math — you need the recognition: when a paper or vendor says 'attention-based,' read 'dot-product similarity deciding what matters.' The humble dot product, all the way down.
notes.title: Dot products, angles, and cosine similarity

notes.body:
A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers — and the operation that matters, matrix multiplication, is just batched dot products. If A is m×n and B is n×p, then C = AB is m×p with C[i,j] = (row i of A)·(column j of B). The inner dimensions must match (n=n); the outer dimensions give the result shape. Worked — the full 2×3 times 3×2, every cell: A = [[1,2,3],[4,5,6]], B = [[7,8],[9,10],[11,12]]. C[1,1] = [1,2,3]·[7,9,11] = 7+18+33 = 58. C[1,2] = [1,2,3]·[8,10,12] = 8+20+36 = 64. C[2,1] = [4,5,6]·[7,9,11] = 28+45+66 = 139. C[2,2] = [4,5,6]·[8,10,12] = 32+50+72 = 154. Result: [[58,64],[139,154]] ✓. Verify one cell independently: 4×7=28, 5×9=45, 6×11=66, sum 139 ✓. Why this operation runs the world: a neural-network layer computes y = Wx + b — the weight matrix W times the input vector x, plus bias. A batch of inputs is a matrix X, and the layer computes WX + b in one shot — thousands of dot products, perfectly parallel, which is exactly what GPUs were built for. Training is also matrix multiplication (gradients flow through the same products backwards). So 'ML at scale' is, computationally, giant matrix multiplications — the math you just did by hand, billions of times per second. Two properties with teeth. Non-commutativity: AB ≠ BA in general — order matters because matrices are transformations and transformations compose in order (rotate-then-scale ≠ scale-then-rotate). Associativity: (AB)C = A(BC) — regroup freely, which is how inference engines reorder products for speed. Identity: AI = IA = A, where I has ones on the diagonal. Worked non-commutativity check: [[1,1],[0,1]]×[[1,0],[1,1]] = [[2,1],[1,1]], but reversed [[1,0],[1,1]]×[[1,1],[0,1]] = [[1,1],[1,2]] — different. Common mistake: multiplying in the wrong order in code (Wx vs xW) — the dimension check (inner match) catches it instantly. Always check dimensions before debugging values.

The batch dimension is where matrices pay for themselves operationally. Scoring one event is a vector dot product; scoring a million events is a matrix multiplication — same math, but the matrix form lets the hardware (GPUs, vector units) parallelize across all million at once instead of looping. The performance difference is not incremental: batched matrix ops run orders of magnitude faster than equivalent Python loops, which is why 'vectorize your code' is the first optimization in every ML pipeline. Worked sense of scale: a layer with a 1024x512 weight matrix scoring a batch of 256 events is one 1024x512x256 multiplication — 134M multiply-adds, executed in milliseconds on a GPU. This shapes system design: collect events into batches for scoring (throughput over latency), size batches to the hardware, and understand that real-time single-event scoring pays the unbatched price. It also shapes attacks: adversarial ML at scale is batched too — the attacker's gradient computations are matrix products, which is why evasion research iterates fast. The matrix is not just notation; it is the unit of computation the entire stack — math, hardware, and economics — is built around.
notes.title: Matrices: batched dot products that run the world

notes.body:
Norms measure size; distances measure separation — together they turn 'unusual' into a number. The L2 (Euclidean) norm is the straight-line length: |v| = √(Σvᵢ²). The L1 (Manhattan) norm sums absolute values: |v|₁ = Σ|vᵢ|. Worked: v=[3,4]. L2 = √(9+16) = √25 = 5. L1 = 3+4 = 7. L2 is the geometry you picture; L1 is the 'city blocks' distance and is more robust to outliers (one huge component dominates L2's square, less so L1's sum). Euclidean distance between points is the L2 norm of their difference: d(a,b) = |a−b|. Worked: a=[1,2], b=[4,6]. a−b = [−3,−4]; |[−3,−4]| = √(9+16) = 5. These are the primitives of anomaly detection: k-nearest-neighbors flags points far from their neighbors; clustering groups nearby points; thresholds on distance-to-centroid catch outliers. Worked security example: baseline a server's hourly feature vectors (connections, bytes, failed logins) for a month; compute the centroid (mean vector) and the typical distance from it. Tonight's vector sits at 6× the typical distance — investigate. That is statistical anomaly detection in one paragraph, and every refinement (Mahalanobis distance, which corrects for feature correlations; z-scores per feature) is a sophistication of this idea. Normalization connects back to the vector note: if bytes range over millions and failed logins over tens, Euclidean distance is 99.99% 'bytes distance' — standardize each feature (subtract mean, divide by standard deviation) so distances reflect shape, not scale. The unit sphere matters too: cosine similarity (previous note) is the dot product of L2-normalized vectors — normalizing to length 1 isolates direction from magnitude. Common mistake: computing distances on unnormalized mixed-scale features and wondering why the detector only sees the biggest feature. Normalize first, distance second — always.

Norms also regularize training — penalizing large weights to keep models simple. L2 regularization adds the squared weight norm to the loss: the optimizer prefers small weights spread across features, which smooths the decision boundary (and, not coincidentally, larger margins — the robustness connection again: L2-regularized models tend to be harder to evade because their boundaries sit farther from the data). L1 regularization adds the absolute norm: it drives unneeded weights exactly to zero, performing feature selection — the model tells you which features it actually uses. Worked intuition: with L1, a 100-feature model might keep 12 nonzero weights — you have learned that 88 features were noise, which is a finding about your data, not just your model. The security angle: inspect the surviving features. If your malware detector's L1 survivors are 'file size' and 'compile timestamp' rather than behavioral features, it is keying on spurious correlations — brittle against trivial attacker changes (recompile, pad the file). Regularization is thus also an audit tool: the weights the model keeps reveal what it learned, and what it learned had better be robust.
notes.title: Norms and distances: measuring 'unusual'

notes.body:
Embeddings are the idea that made modern ML work on language, and the intuition is pure geometry: represent items as dense vectors such that closeness in space means similarity in meaning. 'Dense' matters — unlike one-hot vectors (a million-dimensional vector with a single 1, where every word is equally far from every other), embeddings pack meaning into a few hundred dimensions where geometry works. The similarity measure is usually cosine similarity: similar items point the same way. Worked toy example in 2D — word vectors: malware=[0.9,0.1], ransomware=[0.85,0.15], kitten=[0.1,0.9]. cos(malware, ransomware): dot = 0.9×0.85 + 0.1×0.15 = 0.765+0.015 = 0.78. |malware| = √(0.81+0.01) = √0.82 ≈ 0.9055. |ransomware| = √(0.7225+0.0225) = √0.745 ≈ 0.8631. cos = 0.78/(0.9055×0.8631) = 0.78/0.7816 ≈ 0.998 — nearly identical direction: the model learned they mean nearly the same thing. cos(malware, kitten): dot = 0.9×0.1+0.1×0.9 = 0.18. |kitten| = √0.82 ≈ 0.9055. cos = 0.18/(0.9055×0.9055) = 0.18/0.82 ≈ 0.22 — nearly unrelated. Real embeddings have hundreds of dimensions and subtler geometry (king−man+woman≈queen is the famous party trick — vector arithmetic capturing analogies), but the principle is this toy: direction encodes meaning. Security applications: embed process behaviors, log templates, or binaries, then nearest-neighbor search finds 'things like this known-bad thing' — malware family clustering, phishing template matching, and UEBA all use this shape. Two cautions from earlier modules: embeddings are learned from data, so poisoned training data poisons the geometry (M25/M27); and similarity is not identity — 0.998 similar is not 'the same,' so embedding matches are triage leads, not verdicts. Common mistake: treating embedding distance as a probability or a proof. It is a similarity score — useful for ranking and clustering, never a verdict on its own.

Embeddings have their own adversarial angle, and it connects the module's threads. Because embeddings are learned, they are poisonable: slip crafted samples into training and the geometry shifts — the attacker's malware lands near 'benign' clusters. Because similarity is computed by dot product, they are evadable: small input perturbations move the embedding vector across a nearest-neighbor boundary, so 'nearest known-malware' becomes 'nearest benign utility.' And because embedding spaces are dense and high-dimensional, the attacker has room: the curse of dimensionality means tiny pushes find crossings. Defenses mirror the general toolkit: train embeddings on trusted data, monitor the geometry (has the benign cluster drifted?), and never let a nearest-neighbor match be the verdict — it is a triage lead corroborated by independent signals. There is also a privacy angle: embeddings can leak training data (inversion attacks reconstruct inputs from vectors), so treat stored embeddings of sensitive data with the same care as the data. Geometry is powerful, learned, and attackable — the module's refrain, one last time.
notes.title: Embeddings: similarity as geometry

notes.body:
Now the payoff: the linear classifier from M27's evasion lab, understood geometrically. A linear classifier scores s(x) = w·x + b and predicts positive when s > 0. The decision boundary is where the score is zero: w·x + b = 0. In 2D with w=[1,1], b=−3: x₁+x₂−3=0, i.e., the line x₁+x₂=3 — everything above-right scores positive, below-left negative. The weight vector w is perpendicular to the boundary (it points in the direction of steepest score increase — the gradient direction the M27 attacker followed). The margin — a point's perpendicular distance to the boundary — is |w·x+b|/|w|. Worked: x=[2,2]. Score: 1×2+1×2−3 = 1 > 0, positive class. Margin: |1|/√(1²+1²) = 1/√2 ≈ 0.707. That 0.707 is the robustness budget: any perturbation with a component larger than 0.707 along −w flips the verdict — and M27's δ=[−0.6,−0.6] (norm ≈0.85) spent exactly that budget. Geometry explains the attack completely: the point sat 0.707 from the line, the attacker pushed 0.85 toward it, the point crossed. Support vector machines make the margin the explicit objective: choose the boundary maximizing the minimum margin over training points — the fattest possible street between the classes. Larger margins mean costlier evasion; that is the geometric reason adversarial training (which effectively pushes points away from the boundary) helps. In higher dimensions the boundary is a hyperplane — same equation, w·x+b=0, with w having one component per feature — and the margin formula is unchanged. The 'curse' from M27 also geometric: in high dimensions, most of a point's neighborhood lies near some boundary direction, so small perturbations find crossings easily. Worked 3D extension: w=[1,−1,0.5], b=0, x=[2,1,2]. Score: 2−1+1 = 2 > 0. Margin: 2/√(1+1+0.25) = 2/1.5 ≈ 1.333. Same mechanics, one more dimension. Common mistake: thinking the boundary is where the data is. The boundary is where the model is maximally uncertain — the most attackable real estate in the feature space, which is why attackers live there.

Do not overlook b, the bias term — geometrically it is the boundary's offset from the origin, and operationally it is the prior baked into the model. With b = 0, the boundary passes through the origin: the classifier is 'fair' between classes at the origin. Our b = -3 shifted the line outward: at the origin (x = [0,0]), the score is -3, confidently negative — the model defaults to negative unless the features push hard positive. That default is a choice with consequences: in detection terms, b encodes the tradeoff between false positives and false negatives before any feature is even considered. Raising b (less negative) moves the boundary toward the negative class — more positives, higher recall, more false alarms: it is the threshold knob from statistics, inside the equation. When you inherit a model, inspect b (and the score distribution): a model with an extreme bias is really a mostly-constant classifier wearing a linear costume. And when you train, remember the bias learns the class balance of the training data — train on 99%-benign data and the bias absorbs that prior, which is correct for that population and wrong everywhere else. The bias is the base rate, smuggled into geometry.
notes.title: How a linear classifier draws its line

notes.body:
One more geometric idea, because it powers real anomaly detection: dimensionality reduction and the intuition behind eigenvectors. Real security data has hundreds of features, but the interesting variation often lives in far fewer directions. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) finds those directions: the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix, ordered by eigenvalue (variance captured). Intuition without the full derivation: imagine points scattered mostly along a diagonal line with small perpendicular jitter. The first principal component points along the diagonal (the direction of greatest spread); the second points perpendicular (the jitter direction). Projecting onto just the first component compresses 2D to 1D while keeping the shape that matters. The anomaly-detection trick: learn the principal components of normal traffic, then for each new point measure reconstruction error — project it onto the top components and back, and see how much was lost. Normal points reconstruct well (they fit the learned shape); anomalies reconstruct poorly (they stick out in directions normal data doesn't use). Worked sketch: normal SSH sessions cluster with (bytes, duration) along a line — big transfers take longer. A session with huge bytes and tiny duration reconstructs badly → flag: possible exfiltration-shaped anomaly. That is PCA anomaly detection in a paragraph; your lab implements the core (find the max-variance direction by search). Eigenvectors generally: Av = λv — directions a matrix stretches without rotating, scaled by λ. They appear wherever linear transformations repeat: covariance matrices (PCA), graph adjacency (network centrality — nodes important because important nodes link to them), and Markov chains. You don't need to compute eigendecompositions by hand; you need the intuition — 'the natural axes of the data' — so that when a paper says 'we projected onto the top-k principal components,' you picture the diagonal line, not a black box. And the security caveat, on brand for this course: PCA learns 'normal' from training data — poison that data (M27) and the learned normal includes the attacker's shape. Geometry is powerful, and like every model, it trusts its training data. Common mistake: keeping too few components and discarding the signal, or too many and keeping the noise. The eigenvalue spectrum (how fast variance drops off) tells you where to cut.

Eigenvectors have a second security life beyond PCA: graphs. A network's adjacency matrix has a principal eigenvector — and its entries are eigenvector centrality: nodes score highly when connected to other high-scoring nodes. Worked intuition: in a corporate network graph, the domain controller has high centrality (everything talks to it); a workstation that suddenly jumps in centrality is worth investigating — what is it suddenly connected to? Attack-path analysis uses the same math: the attacker's lateral movement follows high-centrality paths, and defenders harden the nodes whose removal fragments the graph. Even PageRank is an eigenvector computation. The unifying idea: when a matrix describes relationships (covariance between features, adjacency between hosts), its eigenvectors reveal the structure's natural axes — the directions along which the system actually varies or connects. Learn to ask 'what are this matrix's eigenvectors?' about any matrix you meet in security tooling, and you will extract insights the raw numbers hide. It is the same question as PCA, asked of a different matrix — which is why the intuition transfers.
